topics.content:
ELEMENTS OF DESIGN: MEANING, TYPES AND AND USES OF ELEMENTS OF DESIGN
CULTURAL AND CREATIVE ARTS (CCA)
PRIMARY 4 - SECOND TERM - WEEK 1
THEME -  ARTS AND CRAFTS
PREVIOUS LESSON - Mode of Greeting: Meaning of Greeting, Modes of Greeting in Nigeria, Occasions for Greeting and Benefits of Greeting Primary 4 (Basic 4) First Term Week 9 Cultural and Creative Arts
TOPIC - ELEMENTS OF DESIGN
LEARNING
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Types of Elements of Design
3. Uses of the Elements of Design
4. Examples of Elements of Design Around Us
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of design.
2. Explain the meaning of the elements of design.
3. Mention the seven elements of design.
4. State at least five uses of the elements of design.
5. Identify the elements of design in objects found in their environment.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about Modes of Greeting in Nigeria and how different cultural practices help people communicate and show respect.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing pupils to the elements of design, which artists use to create beautiful and meaningful artworks found in homes, schools, clothing, books, and the environment.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Charts showing the elements of design
2. Drawing sheets
3. Pencil and eraser
4. Crayons or coloured pencils
5. Ruler
6. Pictures of artworks, posters, and fabrics
7. Samples of objects showing different shapes, colours, textures, and forms
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Everything around us, such as books, clothes, posters, buildings, and drawings, has been designed using different art elements. Artists combine lines, shapes, colours, textures, forms, spaces, and values to create beautiful and useful artworks.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of design, the elements of design, the types of elements of design, and their uses in creating attractive artworks and designs.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF DESIGN
A Design is the arrangement of lines, shapes, colours, and other art elements to create a beautiful and meaningful work of art.
MEANING OF ELEMENTS OF DESIGN
Elements of design are the basic parts or building blocks that artists use to create artworks and designs.
TYPES OF THE ELEMENTS OF DESIGN
The main elements of design are:
1. Line - A mark made by moving a pencil, pen, or brush from one point to another.
2. Shape - A flat figure with a definite outline, such as a circle, square, or triangle.
3. Colour - Gives beauty, meaning, and attraction to an artwork.
4. Texture - The way the surface of an object feels or looks, such as smooth or rough.
5. Space - The area around, between, or inside objects in an artwork.
6. Form - A three-dimensional (3D) shape, such as a cube, sphere, or cylinder.
7. Value (Tone) - The lightness or darkness of a colour.
LESSON 2 - USES OF THE ELEMENTS OF DESIGN
The elements of design are used to:
1. Create beautiful artworks.
2. Communicate ideas and messages.
3. Decorate homes, schools, and public places.
4. Make posters, cards, and signs attractive.
5. Design clothes and fabrics.
6. Produce books, magazines, and advertisements.
7. Improve creativity and imagination.
8. Make objects more attractive and meaningful.
EXAMPLES OF ELEMENTS OF DESIGN AROUND US
1. Line - Road markings, rulers.
2. Shape - Windows, clocks, books.
3. Colour - Flowers, traffic lights, paintings.
4. Texture - Tree bark, stone, fabric.
5. Space - Classroom, playground.
6. Form - Ball, bottle, box.
7. Value (Tone) - Light and dark parts of a drawing.
LESSON 3 - WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Design is the arrangement of art elements to create a _______.
A. football match
B. beautiful artwork
C. meal
D. road
2. Which of the following is an element of design?
A. Shoe
B. Spoon
C. Table
D. Line
3. Which element of design gives beauty and attraction to an artwork?
A. Colour
B. Space
C. Texture
D. Form
4. Which element of design is a flat figure like a circle or square?
A. Texture
B. Form
C. Shape
D. Value
5. Which element of design refers to how a surface feels or looks?
A. Line
B. Colour
C. Texture
D. Space
B. Fill in the Gaps
Complete the sentences using the words in the box: form, line, shape, space colour
6. A _______ is made by moving a pencil or pen from one point to another.
7. A circle is an example of a _______.
8. _______ makes an artwork attractive and beautiful.
9. A cube is an example of a _______.
10. _______ is the area around or between objects in an artwork.
C. True or False
11. The elements of design are used to create artworks. _______
12. Form describes how a surface feels or looks. _______
13. A triangle is a type of colour. _______
14. Artists use the elements of design to communicate ideas. _______
15. Texture is a three-dimensional (3D) shape. _______
D. Match Column A with Column B.
Column A - Column B
16. Line - A. Lightness or darkness of a colour
17. Shape - B. Mark made by a pencil or pen
18. Texture - C. Flat figure
19. Value (Tone) - D. Surface feel or appearance
20. Form - E. Three-dimensional shape
ANSWER KEYS
1. B - Beautiful artwork
2. D - Line
3. A - Colour
4. C - Shape
5. C - Texture
6. line
7. shape
8. colour
9. form
10. space
11. True
12. False
13. False
14. True
15. False
16. B - Mark made by a pencil or pen
17. C - Flat figure
18. D - Surface feel or appearance
19. A - Lightness or darkness of a colour
20. E - Three-dimensional shape
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that design is the arrangement of art elements to create a beautiful and meaningful artwork. They also learned that the elements of design are the basic parts artists use to create designs and artworks.
Pupils identified the seven elements of design, namely line, shape, colour, texture, space, form, and value (tone).
Furthermore, pupils learned the uses of the elements of design, such as creating beautiful artworks, communicating ideas, decorating objects, designing clothes and fabrics, producing posters and books, and improving creativity.
Finally, pupils identified examples of the elements of design in their surroundings, such as lines on roads, shapes of windows, colours of flowers, textures of fabrics, spaces in classrooms, forms of bottles, and light and dark tones in drawings.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction - The teacher displays different objects such as books, posters, fabrics, bottles, boxes, and drawings. The teacher asks pupils to observe the objects and identify the lines, shapes, colours, and other features they can see.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the objects and identify different elements of design.
Step 2: Meaning of Design and Elements of Design - The teacher explains the meaning of design and elements of design, using simple examples from the classroom and environment.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meanings of design and elements of design in their own words.
Step 3: Types of the Elements of Design - The teacher introduces the seven elements of design: line, shape, colour, texture, space, form, and value (tone). The teacher explains each element with examples.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify each element of design in different objects and artworks.
Step 4: Uses of the Elements of Design - The teacher explains how the elements of design are used to create artworks, decorate objects, communicate ideas, and design books, posters, clothes, and fabrics.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss the uses of the elements of design in everyday life.
Step 5: Practical Activity - The teacher guides pupils to draw simple shapes and colour them, showing the use of lines, shapes, colours, and space in a simple design.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils create simple designs using the elements of design.
Step 6: Group Activity - The teacher divides the class into four groups and assigns the following activities:
- Group 1: Explain the meaning of design and elements of design.
- Group 2: Mention the seven elements of design.
- Group 3: State the uses of the elements of design.
- Group 4: Identify the elements of design in objects found in the classroom.
Each group presents its work to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss the assigned tasks and present their findings.
Step 7: Lesson Summary - The teacher reviews the meaning of design, the elements of design, their types, and their uses.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the lesson.
Step 8: Evaluation - The teacher asks oral and written questions to assess pupils’ understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the evaluation questions and participate actively in the lesson.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Foreign Musical Instruments: Meaning, Types, Classification and Methods of Playing Foreign Musical Instruments Primary 4 (Basic 4) Second Term Week 2 Cultural and Creative Arts
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. Explain the meaning of design.
2. Explain the meaning of the elements of design.
3. Mention the seven elements of design.
4. State at least five uses of the elements of design.
5. Identify the elements of design in objects found in their environment.
6. Draw a simple design using lines, shapes, and colours.

FOREIGN MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS: MEANING, TYPES, CLASSIFICATION AND METHODS OF PLAYING FOREIGN MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS
CULTURAL AND CREATIVE ARTS (CCA)
PRIMARY 4 - SECOND TERM - WEEK
THEME -  MUSIC
PREVIOUS LESSON - Elements of Design: Meaning, Types and Uses of the Elements of Design Primary 4 (Basic 4) Second Term Week 1 Cultural and Creative Arts
TOPIC - FOREIGN MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS
LEARNING
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Types of Foreign Musical Instruments
3. Classification and Methods of Foreign Musical Instruments
4. Uses of Foreign Musical Instruments
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of foreign musical instruments.
2. Mention at least five foreign musical instruments.
3. Classify foreign musical instruments into string, wind, percussion, and keyboard instruments.
4. State the methods of playing different foreign musical instruments.
5. Identify foreign musical instruments from pictures or real objects.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about Elements of Design: Meaning, Types and Uses of the Elements of Design. They understand that different objects are designed for specific purposes and can be identified by their shapes and features.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing pupils to foreign musical instruments, their types, classification, and the different methods of playing them.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Pictures or charts of foreign musical instruments
2. Piano or keyboard (where available)
3. Guitar
4. Recorder or flute
5. Trumpet or saxophone (where available)
6. Drum set or pictures of percussion instruments
7. Flashcards showing the classification of musical instruments
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
People in different countries use different musical instruments to create beautiful music. Some of these instruments, such as the piano, guitar, violin, trumpet, and flute, are used in schools, churches, bands, and orchestras around the world.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of foreign musical instruments, identify different types, classify them into string, wind, percussion, and keyboard instruments, and explain the different methods of playing them.
MEANING OF FOREIGN MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS
Foreign musical instruments are musical instruments that originated from countries outside Nigeria. They are used to produce pleasant sounds and are played in schools, churches, bands, orchestras, and musical performances around the world.
TYPES OF FOREIGN MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS
Some common foreign musical instruments are:
1. Piano - A keyboard instrument played by pressing the keys.
2. Guitar - A string instrument played by plucking or strumming the strings.
3. Violin - A string instrument played with a bow.
4. Trumpet - A wind instrument played by blowing into it.
5. Saxophone - A wind instrument played by blowing through a mouthpiece.
6. Flute - A wind instrument played by blowing across an opening.
7. Clarinet - A wind instrument played by blowing through a reed.
8. Accordion - A keyboard instrument played by pressing the keys or buttons while opening and closing the bellows.
9. Harp - A string instrument played by plucking the strings.
10. Drum Set - A percussion instrument played by striking the drums and cymbals with drumsticks.
CLASSIFICATION OF FOREIGN MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS
Foreign musical instruments can be grouped into four main classes:
1. String Instruments - These instruments produce sound when their strings are plucked, bowed, or struck.
Examples:
- Guitar
- Violin
- Harp
2. Wind Instruments - These instruments produce sound when air is blown into or through them.
Examples:
- Flute
- Trumpet
- Saxophone
- Clarinet
3. Percussion Instruments -
These instruments produce sound when they are struck, shaken, or beaten.
Examples:
- Drum Set
- Cymbals
- Triangle
- Tambourine
4. Keyboard Instruments - These instruments produce sound when their keys are pressed.
Examples:
- Piano
- Organ
- Keyboard
METHODS OF PLAYING FOREIGN MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS
Different foreign musical instruments are played in different ways:
1. Blowing - Flute, trumpet, saxophone, clarinet.
2. Plucking - Guitar and harp.
3. Bowing - Violin.
4. Striking or Beating - Drum set, cymbals, triangle.
5. Pressing the Keys - Piano, organ, keyboard.
USES OF FOREIGN MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS
Foreign musical instruments are used to:
1. Entertain people.
2. Accompany singing and dancing.
3. Play music in churches and schools.
4. Perform in bands and orchestras.
5. Teach music.
6. Develop musical skills and talents.
7. Provide relaxation and enjoyment.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Foreign musical instruments are instruments that come from _______.
A. countries outside Nigeria
B. only villages
C. farms
D. markets

A. Guitar
B. Trumpet
C. Flute
D. Drum Set

A. Piano
B. Violin
C. Saxophone
D. Harp

A. Trumpet
B. Guitar
C. Drum Set
D. Harp

A. Drum Set
B. Flute
C. Violin
D. Clarinet
B. Fill in the Gaps
Complete the sentences using the words in the box: guitar, blowing, piano, violin, percussion
6. A _______ is a keyboard instrument.
7. A _______ is played by plucking the strings.
8. A trumpet is played by _______.
9. A _______ is played with a bow.
10. The drum set belongs to the _______ family of instruments.
C. True or False
11. The guitar is a wind instrument. _______
12. The flute is played by plucking the strings. _______
13. The piano is a percussion instrument. _______
14. The violin is a string instrument. _______
15. Foreign musical instruments can be used in schools and churches. _______
D. Match Column A with Column B.
Column A - Column B
16. Piano - A. Played with a bow
17. Guitar - B. Pressing the keys
18. Violin - C. Blowing

20. Drum Set - E. Plucking the strings
ANSWER KEYS

SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that foreign musical instruments are musical instruments that originated from countries outside Nigeria. They identified common foreign musical instruments such as the piano, guitar, violin, trumpet, saxophone, flute, clarinet, accordion, harp, and drum set.
Pupils also learned that foreign musical instruments are classified into string, wind, percussion, and keyboard instruments.
Furthermore, pupils learned the methods of playing these instruments, including blowing, plucking, bowing, striking or beating, and pressing the keys.
Finally, pupils understood that foreign musical instruments are used for entertainment, education, worship, bands, orchestras, and musical performances.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction - The teacher displays pictures or real examples of foreign musical instruments such as the piano, guitar, violin, trumpet, flute, saxophone, and drum set. The teacher asks pupils if they have seen or heard any of them before.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the instruments and identify those they know.
Step 2: Meaning of Foreign Musical Instruments - The teacher explains that foreign musical instruments are musical instruments that originated from countries outside Nigeria.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of foreign musical instruments in their own words.
Step 3: Types and Classification of Foreign Musical Instruments - The teacher introduces the different types and classifies them into string, wind, percussion, and keyboard instruments, giving examples of each.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils classify the musical instruments into their correct groups.
Step 4: Methods of Playing Foreign Musical Instruments - The teacher demonstrates or explains how different instruments are played by blowing, plucking, bowing, striking or beating, and pressing the keys.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the correct method of playing each instrument.
Step 5: Uses of Foreign Musical Instruments - The teacher explains the uses of foreign musical instruments in entertainment, worship, schools, bands, orchestras, and music education.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention places where foreign musical instruments are used.
Step 6: Group Activity - The teacher divides the class into four groups and assigns the following activities:
- Group 1: Explain the meaning of foreign musical instruments.
- Group 2: Mention at least five foreign musical instruments.
- Group 3: Classify the instruments into string, wind, percussion, and keyboard groups.
- Group 4: State the methods of playing the different foreign musical instruments.
Each group presents its work to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss the assigned tasks and present their findings.
Step 7: Lesson Summary - The teacher reviews the meaning, types, classification, methods of playing, and uses of foreign musical instruments.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the lesson.
Step 8: Evaluation - The teacher asks oral and written questions to assess pupils’ understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the evaluation questions and participate actively in the lesson.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

topics.content:
TRADITIONAL DANCE: MEANING AND FEATURES OF TRADITIONAL DANCE IN NIGERIA
CULTURAL AND CREATIVE ARTS (CCA)
PRIMARY 4 - SECOND TERM - WEEK 3
THEME -  MUSIC
PREVIOUS LESSON - Foreign Musical Instruments: Meaning, Types, Classification and Methods of Playing Foreign Musical Instruments Primary 4 (Basic 4) Second Term Week 2 Cultural and Creative Arts
TOPIC - FEATURES OF NIGERIAN TRADITIONAL DANCE
LEARNING
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Features of Traditional Dance
3. Examples of Traditional Dance in Nigeria
4. Importance of Traditional Dance
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of traditional dance.
2. Mention at least five features of traditional dance in Nigeria.
3. Identify at least three examples of traditional dances in Nigeria.
4. State at least five importance of traditional dance.
5. Demonstrate simple traditional dance steps.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about Foreign Musical Instruments: Meaning, Types, Classification, and Methods of Playing Foreign Musical Instruments. They understand that music and musical instruments are used to accompany songs and dances.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing pupils to traditional dance, its features, and its importance in Nigerian culture.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Pictures or charts of Nigerian traditional dances
2. Traditional musical instruments (or pictures)
3. Audio or video recordings of traditional dances (where available)
4. Traditional costumes (or pictures)
5. Flashcards showing the features of traditional dance
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.

2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Nigeria has many traditional dances that are performed during festivals, weddings, naming ceremonies, and other cultural events. These dances are accompanied by traditional music, colourful costumes, and special dance steps that reflect the customs and traditions of different ethnic groups.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of traditional dance, identify its features, mention examples of traditional dances in Nigeria, and explain their importance in preserving Nigerian culture.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF TRADITIONAL DANCE
Traditional dance is a cultural dance performed by people to express their customs, beliefs, history, and way of life. It is usually performed during festivals, ceremonies, and other special occasions.
FEATURES OF TRADITIONAL DANCE IN NIGERIA
Traditional dances in Nigeria have the following features:
1. It reflects culture and tradition of the people.
2. It is performed during special occasions such as festivals, weddings, and naming ceremonies.
3. It uses traditional musical instruments like talking drums, gongs, and rattles.
4. Dancers wear traditional costumes that represent their culture.
5. It involves rhythmic body movements and coordinated dance steps.
6. It is performed in groups or individually, depending on the dance.
7. It tells stories or expresses feelings through movement.
8. It promotes unity and cooperation among community members.
9. It is passed from one generation to another.
10. It entertains and educates people about their cultural heritage.
LESSON 2 - EXAMPLES OF TRADITIONAL DANCES IN NIGERIA
1. Bata Dance - Yoruba
2. Atilogwu Dance - Igbo
3. Koroso Dance - Hausa
4. Swange Dance - Tiv
5. Ekombi Dance - Efik
IMPORTANCE OF TRADITIONAL DANCE
Traditional dance helps to:
1. Preserve Nigerian culture.
2. Entertain people.
3. Unite communities.
4. Teach cultural values.
5. Celebrate important events.
6. Promote physical fitness.
7. Develop talents and creativity.

SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that traditional dance is a cultural dance performed to express the customs, beliefs, history, and way of life of a people.
Pupils identified the features of traditional dance in Nigeria, such as the use of traditional costumes, traditional musical instruments, rhythmic body movements, cultural expressions, storytelling, and performances during festivals and ceremonies.
Furthermore, pupils learned examples of Nigerian traditional dances, including Bata Dance (Yoruba), Atilogwu Dance (Igbo), Koroso Dance (Hausa), Swange Dance (Tiv), and Ekombi Dance (Efik).
Finally, pupils understood that traditional dance helps to preserve culture, entertain people, promote unity, teach cultural values, celebrate important occasions, develop talents, and promote physical fitness.
PRESENTATION

Step 1: Introduction - The teacher displays pictures or plays a short video of Nigerian traditional dances. The teacher asks pupils if they have seen or participated in any traditional dance.

Step 2: Meaning of Traditional Dance - The teacher explains that traditional dance is a cultural dance performed to express the customs, beliefs, history, and way of life of a people.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of traditional dance in their own words.

Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the features of traditional dance from pictures or demonstrations.
Step 4: Examples and Importance of Traditional Dance - The teacher introduces examples of traditional dances in Nigeria, such as Bata, Atilogwu, Koroso, Swange, and Ekombi, and explains their importance in preserving culture, promoting unity, and entertaining people.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention examples of traditional dances and discuss their importance.
Step 5: Practical Demonstration - The teacher demonstrates simple traditional dance steps or invites pupils to perform simple dance movements while traditional music is played.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils practise simple traditional dance steps individually or in groups.
Step 6: Group Activity - The teacher divides the class into four groups and assigns the following activities:
- Group 1: Explain the meaning of traditional dance.
- Group 2: Mention the features of traditional dance.
- Group 3: Identify examples of traditional dances in Nigeria.
- Group 4: State the importance of traditional dance.
Each group presents its work to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss the assigned tasks and present their findings.
Step 7: Lesson Summary - The teacher reviews the meaning, features, examples, and importance of traditional dance.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the lesson.
Step 8: Evaluation - The teacher asks oral and written questions to assess pupils’ understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the evaluation questions and participate actively in the lesson.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

2. Mention at least five materials found in the environment.
3. Differentiate between natural and man-made materials found in the environment.
4. State at least five ways of caring for the environment.
5. Demonstrate good environmental sanitation practices in the school and home.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about Traditional Dance: Meaning and Features of Traditional Dance in Nigeria. They understand that cultural activities take place in the community and require a clean and safe environment.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing pupils to the environment, the materials found in it, and the importance of caring for the environment.

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Everything around us, such as trees, flowers, soil, buildings, roads, water, and animals, forms part of our environment. A clean and healthy environment helps people live happily and prevents diseases. Everyone has a responsibility to keep the environment clean and safe.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of the environment, identify materials found in the environment, and explain ways of caring for the environment.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF ENVIRONMENT
The environment is everything around us. It includes all the living and non-living things in our surroundings, such as people, animals, plants, air, water, land, buildings, and roads.

LEARNING OBJECTIVES

1. Explain the meaning of the principles of design.
2. Mention at least five principles of design.
3. Explain the different types of the principles of design.
4. State at least five uses of the principles of design.
5. Identify the principles of design in simple artworks and objects around them.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about Care of the Environment: Meaning of Environment, Materials Found in the Environment, and Ways of Caring for the Environment. They also learned about the elements of design, such as line, shape, colour, texture, space, form, and value.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing the principles of design, which are the rules used to arrange the elements of design to produce beautiful and meaningful artworks.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Every beautiful artwork is carefully arranged to make it attractive and meaningful. Artists do not place colours, shapes, or lines randomly; they follow certain rules to create neat and balanced designs. These rules are called the principles of design.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of the principles of design, identify their types, and explain their uses in creating beautiful artworks and designs.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF THE PRINCIPLES OF DESIGN
The principles of design are the basic rules or guidelines artists use to arrange the elements of design to create attractive, balanced, and meaningful artworks.
TYPES OF THE PRINCIPLES OF DESIGN
The main principles of design are:
1. Balance - Arranging objects so that the artwork looks stable and evenly distributed.
2. Contrast - Using different colours, shapes, sizes, or textures to make parts of an artwork stand out.
3. Emphasis - Making one part of an artwork more noticeable than the others. This is also called the centre of interest.
4. Rhythm - Repeating lines, shapes, colours, or patterns to create a sense of movement.
5. Pattern - Repeating the same design, shape, or decoration over and over again.
6. Unity - Combining all parts of an artwork so they work together as one complete design.
7. Proportion - The correct size relationship between the parts of an artwork.
LESSON 2 - USES OF THE PRINCIPLES OF DESIGN
The principles of design are used to:
1. Make artworks attractive and beautiful.
2. Organise the elements of design properly.
3. Create balance in artworks.
4. Draw attention to important parts of a design.
5. Improve creativity and imagination.
6. Make posters, books, clothes, and decorations more appealing.
7. Help artists communicate ideas clearly.
8. Produce neat and meaningful designs.
IMPORTANCE OF THE PRINCIPLES OF DESIGN
The principles of design help artists to:
1. Create attractive artworks.
2. Produce balanced and organised designs.
3. Express ideas and emotions.
4. Improve the quality of artworks.
5. Make artworks easy to understand.

SUMMARY

Pupils identified the main principles of design, namely balance, contrast, emphasis, rhythm, pattern, unity, and proportion.
Furthermore, pupils learned the uses of the principles of design, such as making artworks attractive, organising the elements of design properly, creating balance, drawing attention to important parts of an artwork, improving creativity, and producing neat and meaningful designs.
Finally, pupils understood that artists use the principles of design to create beautiful, balanced, organised, and effective artworks that communicate ideas clearly.

Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the different principles of design in the sample artworks.

Step 5: Practical Activity - The teacher guides pupils to draw and colour a simple design, showing the use of balance, pattern, contrast, and unity.

Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the lesson.

2. Mention at least five traditional Nigerian musical instruments.
3. Identify the tribes or ethnic groups associated with selected Nigerian musical instruments.
4. Describe the sounds produced by different traditional Nigerian musical instruments.

ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about Principles of Design: Meaning, Types and Uses of the Principles of Design. They also learned about foreign musical instruments and their methods of playing.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing pupils to traditional Nigerian musical instruments, the tribes that use them, and the different sounds they produce.

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Nigeria is home to many ethnic groups, and each group has its own traditional musical instruments. These instruments are used during festivals, weddings, traditional dances, religious ceremonies, and other cultural events. Each instrument produces a unique sound and represents the culture of the people who use it.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of Nigerian musical instruments, identify traditional Nigerian musical instruments, state the tribes associated with them, and describe the sounds they produce.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF NIGERIAN MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS
Nigerian musical instruments are musical instruments that originated in Nigeria and are used by different ethnic groups to produce music during festivals, ceremonies, worship, entertainment, and cultural celebrations.
TRADITIONAL NIGERIAN MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS AND THE SOUNDS THEY PRODUCE
Traditional Musical Instrument - Tribe/Ethnic Group - Sound Produced
1. Talking Drum (Gangan/Dùndún) - Yoruba - Talking or rhythmic drum sounds (“dum-dum”, “ton-ton”)
2. Bata Drum - Yoruba - Deep rhythmic beats
3. Ekwe (Wooden Slit Drum) - Igbo - Sharp knocking or hollow wooden sounds
4. Ogene (Metal Gong) - Igbo - Clear metallic ringing sound (“gong-gong”)
5. Shekere - Yoruba - Rattling or shaking sound
6. Udu (Clay Pot Drum) - Igbo - Deep hollow booming sound
7. Kakaki (Long Trumpet) - Hausa - Loud trumpet-like sound
8. Goje (Traditional Fiddle) - Hausa/Fulani - Soft, high-pitched string sound
9. Oja (Flute) - Igbo - Soft whistling or blowing sound
10. Ekombi Drum - Efik - Rhythmic drum beats used to accompany the Ekombi dance

1. Entertain people.

SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that Nigerian musical instruments are traditional musical instruments that originated in Nigeria and are used by different ethnic groups during festivals, ceremonies, worship, entertainment, and cultural celebrations.
Pupils identified various traditional Nigerian musical instruments, including the Talking Drum (Gangan/Dùndún), Bata Drum, Ekwe, Ogene, Shekere, Udu, Kakaki, Goje, Oja, and Ekombi Drum.
They also learned the tribes associated with these instruments and the different sounds they produce, such as talking, ringing, rattling, booming, blowing, and rhythmic drum beats.
Finally, pupils understood that Nigerian musical instruments are important for entertainment, traditional dances, cultural festivals, communication, worship, music education, and preserving Nigeria’s cultural heritage.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction - The teacher displays pictures or real traditional Nigerian musical instruments such as the Talking Drum, Bata Drum, Ekwe, Ogene, Shekere, Udu, Kakaki, Goje, and Oja. The teacher asks pupils if they have seen or heard any of these instruments before.

Step 3: Traditional Nigerian Musical Instruments, Their Tribes, and Sounds - The teacher introduces the different traditional Nigerian musical instruments, the ethnic groups that use them, and the sounds they produce.

Step 4: Uses of Nigerian Musical Instruments - The teacher explains that Nigerian musical instruments are used during festivals, traditional dances, weddings, religious ceremonies, cultural celebrations, entertainment, and for communication in some communities.

BASIC MOVEMENTS IN DANCE: MEANING AND COMPONENTS OF BASIC MOVEMENTS IN DANCE
CULTURAL AND CREATIVE ARTS (CCA)
PRIMARY 4 - SECOND TERM - WEEK 8
THEME -  ARTS AND CRAFTS
PREVIOUS LESSON - Nigerian Musical Instruments: Meaning, Traditional Nigerian Musical Instruments and the Sounds They Produce Primary 4 (Basic 4) Second Term Week 6 Cultural and Creative Arts
TOPIC - BASIC MOVEMENTS IN DANCE
LEARNING
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Components of Basic Movements in Dance
3. Examples of Basic Movements in Dance

LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of basic movements in dance.
2. Mention the components of basic movements in dance.
3. Identify the examples of basic dance movements.
4. Demonstrate simple basic dance movements correctly.
5. State the importance of basic movements in dance.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about Nigerian Musical Instruments: Meaning, Traditional Nigerian Musical Instruments, and the Sounds They Produce. They know that traditional musical instruments provide the rhythm and beats used during dance performances.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing pupils to the basic movements in dance and the components that make dance performances meaningful and enjoyable.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Pictures or charts showing different dance movements
2. Audio player or drum for dance rhythm
3. Traditional musical instruments (or pictures)
4. Flashcards showing the components of dance

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Whenever people dance, they move different parts of their bodies in various ways to match the rhythm of the music. These simple actions, such as walking, jumping, clapping, swaying, and turning, are called basic dance movements. Learning these movements helps us dance well, keep fit, and express our feelings.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of basic movements in dance, identify their components, recognise examples of basic dance movements, and practise simple dance steps.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF BASIC MOVEMENTS IN DANCE
Basic movements in dance are the simple body actions or steps used to create and perform a dance. These movements help dancers express feelings, ideas, and emotions through body movements.
COMPONENTS OF BASIC MOVEMENTS IN DANCE
The main components of basic movements in dance are:
1. Body - The body is the main tool used for dancing. Different parts of the body, such as the head, hands, arms, legs, feet, and waist, move during a dance.
2. Space - Space refers to the area where a dancer moves. A dancer may move forward, backward, sideways, up, down, or around the performance area.
3. Time - Time is the speed or rhythm of a dance movement. A dancer may move slowly, quickly, or at a moderate pace, following the beat of the music.
4. Energy (Force) - Energy is the amount of strength used while dancing. Movements may be gentle, light, strong, or powerful.
5. Relationship - Relationship refers to how a dancer moves with other dancers, objects, or the audience during a performance.
LESSON 2 - EXAMPLES OF BASIC DANCE MOVEMENTS
1. Walking - Moving from one place to another with regular steps while following the rhythm of the music.
2. Running - Moving faster than walking to add speed and excitement to a dance.
3. Jumping - Pushing the body off the ground with both feet and landing safely.
4. Hopping - Jumping repeatedly on one foot while keeping balance.
5. Skipping - Moving forward with a light step and hop, usually to the beat of the music.
6. Bending - Lowering or folding parts of the body, such as the knees, waist, or arms, during a dance.
7. Stretching - Extending the arms, legs, or body to increase flexibility and create graceful movements.
8. Turning (Twisting) - Rotating the body around in a circle or twisting the waist while dancing.
9. Clapping - Bringing the hands together to produce rhythm and accompany dance movements.
10. Swaying - Moving the body gently from side to side in time with the music.
IMPORTANCE OF BASIC MOVEMENTS IN DANCE
Basic movements in dance help to:
1. Develop body coordination.
2. Improve balance and flexibility.
3. Promote physical fitness.
4. Build confidence.
5. Express feelings and emotions.
6. Encourage teamwork and cooperation.
7. Prepare learners for more advanced dance skills.

SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that basic movements in dance are simple body actions or steps used to create and perform dances. These movements help dancers express ideas, feelings, and emotions through body movement.
Pupils identified the components of basic movements in dance, namely body, space, time, energy, and relationship.
Furthermore, pupils learned examples of basic dance movements such as walking, running, jumping, hopping, skipping, bending, stretching, turning (twisting), clapping, and swaying.
Finally, pupils understood that basic movements in dance help to improve body coordination, balance, flexibility, physical fitness, confidence, teamwork, and prepare dancers for more advanced dance skills.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction - The teacher plays a simple piece of music or beats a drum and asks pupils to move their bodies freely to the rhythm. The teacher then asks what movements they made while dancing.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils dance freely and mention movements such as walking, jumping, clapping, and swaying.
Step 2: Meaning of Basic Movements in Dance - The teacher explains that basic movements in dance are simple body actions or steps used to create and perform a dance.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of basic movements in dance in their own words.
Step 3: Components of Basic Movements in Dance - The teacher explains the components of basic movements in dance:
- Body
- Space
- Time
- Energy
- Relationship
The teacher demonstrates each component using simple dance activities.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify and demonstrate each component through guided movements.
Step 4: Examples of Basic Dance Movements - The teacher demonstrates basic dance movements such as walking, running, jumping, hopping, skipping, bending, stretching, turning (twisting), clapping, and swaying.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils imitate and practise each movement correctly.
Step 5: Practical Demonstration - The teacher leads pupils in a simple dance routine that combines different basic movements while music is played.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils perform the dance routine individually or in pairs.
Step 6: Group Activity - The teacher divides the class into four groups and assigns the following activities:
- Group 1: Explain the meaning of basic movements in dance.
- Group 2: Mention the components of basic movements in dance.
- Group 3: Demonstrate five basic dance movements.
- Group 4: State the importance of basic movements in dance.
Each group presents its work to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss the assigned tasks, demonstrate the movements, and present their findings.
Step 7: Lesson Summary - The teacher reviews the meaning, components, examples, and importance of basic movements in dance.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the lesson.
Step 8: Evaluation - The teacher asks oral and written questions to assess pupils’ understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the evaluation questions and participate actively in the lesson.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

THEME -  ARTS AND CRAFTS

LEARNING
1. Introduction
2. Meaning, Types and Sources of Colours
3. Sources and Uses of Colours
4. Wheel Colours and Painting
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of colour.
2. Identify different types of colours (primary, secondary, and tertiary colours).
3. Mention the sources of colours.
4. State the uses of colours.
5. Explain the meaning of the colour wheel.
6. Demonstrate simple colour mixing and produce a simple painting using colours.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about Basic Movements in Dance: Meaning and Components of Basic Movements in Dance. They have also learned about the elements and principles of design, which include colour as an important element used in artworks.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing pupils to the meaning, types, sources, and uses of colours, the colour wheel, and painting.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Colour wheel chart
2. Posters showing primary, secondary, and tertiary colours
3. Watercolour or poster paint
4. Paintbrushes
5. Crayons and coloured pencils
6. Palette or mixing tray
7. Water container
8. Drawing paper or cardboard
9. Pictures of colourful objects in the environment
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Every day we see different colours around us, such as the blue sky, green leaves, red flowers, yellow sun, and colourful clothes. Colours make our environment beautiful and help us identify different objects easily. Artists also use colours to create attractive paintings and designs.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of colour, the types, sources, and uses of colours, the colour wheel, and how colours are used in painting.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF COLOURS IN OUR ENVIRONMENT
Colours in our environment are the different colours we see around us in nature and in man-made objects. They are found in things such as the sky, flowers, trees, animals, fruits, buildings, clothes, vehicles, and artworks. Colours make our surroundings beautiful, attractive, and easy to recognise.
EXAMPLES OF COLOURS IN OUR ENVIRONMENT
1. Red - Roses, tomatoes, ripe apples, stop signs
2. Yellow - Sunflower, ripe bananas, the sun
3. Blue - Sky, rivers, oceans
4. Green - Leaves, grass, vegetables
5. Orange - Oranges, carrots
6. Purple (Violet) - Some flowers, grapes
6. Black - Charcoal, tyres
7. White - Clouds, paper, milk
8. Brown - Tree trunks, soil, wood
LESSON 2 - MEANING OF COLOUR
Colour is the appearance of an object when light reflects from it. Colour makes objects beautiful, attractive, and easy to identify in our environment.
TYPES OF COLOURS
1. Primary Colours
These are the basic colours that cannot be made by mixing other colours.
- Red
- Yellow
- Blue
2. Secondary Colours
These are colours formed by mixing two primary colours.
- Green (Blue + Yellow)
- Orange (Red + Yellow)
- Purple/Violet (Red + Blue)
3. Tertiary Colours
These are colours formed by mixing a primary colour with a neighbouring secondary colour.
- Red-Orange
- Yellow-Orange
- Yellow-Green
- Blue-Green
- Blue-Violet
- Red-Violet
LESSON 3 - SOURCES OF COLOURS
Colours can be obtained from different sources, such as:
1. Natural Sources
- Flowers
- Leaves
- Fruits
- Soil
- Charcoal
- Clay
- Trees
- Minerals
2. Artificial (Man-made) Sources
- Paint
- Crayons
- Coloured pencils
- Markers
- Fabric dyes
- Printing ink
- Watercolour
- Poster colour
USES OF COLOURS
Colours are used to:
1. Beautify our surroundings.
2. Decorate homes, schools, and public places.
3. Paint pictures and artworks.
4. Design clothes and fabrics.
5. Make signs and posters attractive.
6. Identify objects easily.
7. Express feelings and emotions.
8. Improve creativity in art and design.
LESSON 4 (AVAILABLE FREE PERIOD) - COLOUR WHEEL
A colour wheel is a circular chart that shows the relationship between colours.
The colour wheel consists of:
1. Primary Colours: Red, Yellow, Blue
2. Secondary Colours: Green, Orange, Purple (Violet)
3. Tertiary Colours: Red-Orange, Yellow-Orange, Yellow-Green, Blue-Green, Blue-Violet, Red-Violet
PAINTING
Painting is the art of applying colours to a surface such as paper, canvas, wood, or walls using brushes, fingers, sponges, or other tools to create beautiful pictures and designs.
Materials for Painting
1. Paint
2. Paintbrush
3. Water
4. Palette
5. Drawing paper or cardboard
6. Pencil
7. Eraser
IMPORTANCE OF COLOUR AND PAINTING
Colour and painting help to:
1. Beautify artworks and the environment.
2. Develop creativity and imagination.
3. Express ideas and emotions.
4. Improve artistic skills.
5. Make learning interesting and enjoyable.
6. Preserve culture through art.
7. Create attractive designs and decorations.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions

SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that colour is the appearance of an object when light reflects from it. Colours make our environment beautiful, attractive, and easy to identify.
Pupils identified the types of colours, namely primary colours (Red, Yellow, and Blue), secondary colours (Green, Orange, and Purple/Violet), and tertiary colours, which are formed by mixing a primary colour with a neighbouring secondary colour.
Furthermore, pupils learned the sources of colours, which include natural sources (such as flowers, leaves, fruits, clay, and minerals) and artificial sources (such as paint, crayons, coloured pencils, and dyes). They also discussed the uses of colours in decoration, painting, communication, and identification.
Finally, pupils learned that a colour wheel is a circular chart that shows the relationship among colours, and that painting is the art of applying colours to a surface to create beautiful pictures and designs.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction - The teacher displays colourful objects such as flowers, fruits, clothes, crayons, and charts. The teacher asks pupils to identify the colours they can see.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the objects and mention different colours such as red, yellow, blue, green, orange, and purple.
Step 2: Meaning of Colour - The teacher explains that colour is the appearance of an object when light reflects from it. Colours make objects attractive and easy to identify.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of colour in their own words.
Step 3: Types, Sources, and Uses of Colours - The teacher introduces the types of colours:
- Primary colours

The teacher also explains the natural and artificial sources of colours and discusses their uses in everyday life.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify different colours, classify them, and state their sources and uses.
Step 4: Colour Wheel - The teacher displays a colour wheel and explains how primary colours are mixed to produce secondary colours and how tertiary colours are formed.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the colour wheel and identify the primary, secondary, and tertiary colours.
Step 5: Painting Activity - The teacher demonstrates how to mix colours and use a paintbrush to produce a simple painting.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mix colours and create a simple painting using paint, crayons, or coloured pencils.
Step 6: Group Activity - The teacher divides the class into four groups and assigns the following activities:
- Group 1: Explain the meaning of colour.
- Group 2: Identify the types of colours with examples.
- Group 3: State the sources and uses of colours.
- Group 4: Draw and label a simple colour wheel or produce a simple painting.
Each group presents its work to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss the assigned tasks and present their findings.
Step 7: Lesson Summary - The teacher reviews the meaning, types, sources, and uses of colours, the colour wheel, and painting.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the lesson.
Step 8: Evaluation - The teacher asks oral and written questions to assess pupils’ understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the evaluation questions and participate actively in the lesson.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

SONGS/MUSIC WITH NIGERIAN IDENTITY: NIGERIAN MUSIC COMPOSERS, THEIR CONTRIBUTIONS AND MUSIC COMPOSITION
CULTURAL AND CREATIVE ARTS (CCA)

THEME -  MUSIC

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of songs and music with Nigerian identity.
2. Explain the meaning of a music composer.
3. Mention at least five Nigerian music composers.
4. State the contributions of Nigerian music composers.
5. Explain the meaning of music composition.

ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about Colour in Our Environment: Meaning, Types, Sources and Uses of Colours, Colour Wheel, and Painting. They have also learned about Nigerian musical instruments and basic movements in dance.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing pupils to songs and music with Nigerian identity, Nigerian music composers, their contributions, and the process of music composition.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Nigeria is blessed with many talented musicians and composers who create songs that promote our culture, traditions, languages, peace, and unity. Many of these songs are sung in schools, churches, communities, and during national celebrations. The people who write and arrange these songs are called music composers.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of songs and music with Nigerian identity, identify Nigerian music composers, explain their contributions, and understand the meaning and process of music composition.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF SONGS AND MUSIC WITH NIGERIAN IDENTITY
Songs and music with Nigerian identity are songs and musical works that reflect the culture, traditions, languages, values, and way of life of the Nigerian people. They promote Nigeria’s cultural heritage and national unity.
MEANING OF A MUSIC COMPOSERS
A music composer is a person who creates or writes songs and music by arranging lyrics, melodies, rhythms, and musical notes.
MUSIC COMPOSERS AND THEIR CONTRIBUTIONS
1. Lazarus Ekwueme
- Composed many Nigerian choral songs.
- Promoted Nigerian indigenous music.
- Trained many musicians.
2. Ayo Bankole
- Combined Nigerian traditional music with classical music.
- Promoted Yoruba culture through music.
- Wrote many piano and choral compositions.
3. Fela Anikulapo Kuti
- Created and popularised Afrobeat music.
- Used music to educate people about social issues.
- Promoted Nigerian music worldwide.
4. Bongos Ikwue
- Composed songs that promote peace, love, and unity.
- Contributed to the growth of Nigerian popular music.
5. Onyeka Onwenu
- Promoted Nigerian culture through music.
- Sang songs that encourage unity and patriotism.
- Inspired young musicians.
CONTRIBUTIONS OF NIGERIAN MUSIC COMPOSERS
Nigerian music composers:
1. Promote Nigerian culture and traditions.
2. Preserve indigenous languages through songs.
3. Entertain people.
4. Teach moral values.
5. Promote peace, unity, and patriotism.
6. Inspire young musicians.
7. Make Nigerian music known around the world.
LESSON 2 - MEANING OF MUSIC COMPOSITION
Music composition is the process of creating or writing a new song or piece of music by arranging lyrics, melody, rhythm, and harmony.
Steps in Music Composition
Choose a topic or message.

2. Create a melody.
3. Add rhythm and beat.
4. Practise and improve the song.

Music composition helps to:

2. Preserve culture and traditions.
3. Educate people.

Pupils also learned that a music composer is a person who creates or writes songs by arranging lyrics, melody, rhythm, and harmony.
Furthermore, pupils identified some Nigerian music composers, including Lazarus Ekwueme, Ayo Bankole, Fela Anikulapo Kuti, Bongos Ikwue, and Onyeka Onwenu, and discussed their contributions to the growth and promotion of Nigerian music and culture.
Finally, pupils learned that music composition is the process of creating or writing a song. They also understood that music helps to promote culture, preserve traditions, educate people, entertain audiences, encourage creativity, and foster peace and national unity.

To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:

CREATIN6A PLAY WITH THE THEME OF HONESTY, INTEGRITY AND RIGHT ATTITUDE TO WORK
CULTURAL AND CREATIVE ARTS (CCA)
PRIMARY 4 - SECOND TERM - WEEK 11
THEME -  DRAMA
PREVIOUS LESSON - Songs and Music with Nigerian Identity: Nigerian Music Composers, Their Contributions and Music Composition Primary 4 (Basic 4) Second Term Week 10 Cultural and Creative Arts
TOPIC - CREATING A PLAY
LEARNING
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of Honesty, Integrity and Right Attitude
3. Steps in Creating Play
4. Creating a Play with the Themes of Honesty, Integrity and Right Attitude
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of a play.
2. Explain the themes of honesty, integrity, and right attitude to work.
3. Identify the characters and setting of a simple play.
4. Create a simple play based on honesty, integrity, or right attitude to work.
5. Act and present a simple play before the class.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about Songs and Music with Nigerian Identity, Nigerian music composers, and music composition. They have also learned about Drama and Theatre, including the meaning and elements of drama.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils how to create and perform a simple play based on the themes of honesty, integrity, and right attitude to work.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Simple play scripts
2. Flashcards showing the words Honesty, Integrity, and Right Attitude to Work
3. Charts illustrating good moral behaviour
4. Costumes or simple props (school bag, books, broom, chair, etc.)
5. Pictures of drama activ ities
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Every day, we make choices that show whether we are honest, have integrity, and have the right attitude to work. Drama and plays help us learn these good values in an interesting and practical way. By acting out different situations, we can understand the importance of telling the truth, doing the right thing, and working hard.
In this lesson, pupils will learn how to create and perform simple plays with the themes of honesty, integrity, and right attitude to work, while developing confidence, teamwork, and good moral values.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF A PLAY
A play is a story written to be acted on a stage or before an audience. It has characters, dialogue, and actions that communicate a message or teach a lesson.
MEANING OF HONESTY
Honesty means always telling the truth, being sincere, and not cheating, stealing, or deceiving others.
Examples of Honesty
1. Telling the truth even when it is difficult.
2. Returning a lost item to its owner.
3. Admitting one’s mistakes.
4. Refusing to cheat during a test.
MEANING OF INTEGRITY
Integrity means doing the right thing at all times, even when no one is watching. A person with integrity is honest, trustworthy, and has strong moral values.
Examples of Integrity
1. Keeping promises.
2. Refusing to take what does not belong to you.
3. Obeying rules without being forced.
4. Being fair to everyone.
MEANING OF RIGHT ATTITUDE TO WORK
Right attitude to work means doing every task willingly, responsibly, carefully, honestly, and on time.
Examples of Right Attitude to Work
1. Completing assignments on time.
2. Keeping the classroom clean.
3. Respecting teachers and classmates.
4. Working hard during class activities.
5. Taking good care of school property.
LESSON 2 - STEPS IN CREATING A PLAY
1. Choose a theme (Honesty, Integrity, or Right Attitude to Work).
2. Decide on the characters.
3. Write a simple story with a beginning, middle, and ending.
4. Write the dialogue for each character.
5. Rehearse the play.
6. Perform the play before an audience.
SIMPLE PLAY
1. CREATING A PLAY WITH THE THEME: THE HONEST PUPILS
Title: The Honest Pupil
Characters: Teacher, Tunde, Ada, Narrator
Narrator: One day, Tunde found a wallet in the classroom.
- Tunde: I found this wallet. I will give it to the teacher.
- Teacher: Thank you, Tunde. You have shown honesty and integrity.
- Ada: Tunde has set a good example for all of us.
- Teacher: We should always be honest and have the right attitude to work.
Narrator: Everyone clapped for Tunde because he did the right thing.
Moral Lesson: Honesty, integrity, and hard work bring respect and trust.
2. CREATING A PLAY WITH THE THEME OF INTEGRITY
Title: Doing the Right Thing
Characters: Narrator, Teacher, Tola, Musa
Narrator: One morning, the teacher asked the pupils to submit their homework.
- Teacher: Good morning, class. Please submit your homework.
- Musa: (Whispers to Tola) I forgot to do my homework. Can I copy yours?
- Tola: No, Musa. That would not be honest. You should tell the teacher the truth.
- Musa: You are right. I will be truthful.
- Teacher: Musa, where is your homework?
- Musa: I am sorry, Ma. I forgot to do it. I will complete it today and submit it tomorrow.
- Teacher: Thank you for telling the truth. You have shown integrity by being honest instead of copying someone else’s work.
- Tola: Doing the right thing is always better than cheating.
Narrator: Musa learned that people with integrity tell the truth and do the right thing, even when it is difficult.
Moral Lesson: Always do the right thing, be honest, and show integrity in e verything you do.
CREATING A PLAY WITH THE THEME: RIGHT ATTITUDE TO WORK
Title: A Good Worker
Characters: Narrator, Teacher, Chidi, Amina
Narrator: The teacher asked the pupils to clean the classroom before the lesson began.
- Teacher: Children, please sweep the classroom and arrange your desks neatly.
- Amina: Yes, Ma. Let us start now.
- Chidi: I don’t feel like working. I will just sit down.
- Amina: Chidi, we should all do our part. A good pupil works hard and helps others.
- Chidi: You are right. I will help too. (Chidi joins Amina in sweeping and arranging the classroom.)
- Teacher: Well done, children! You worked together and completed the task on time.
- Chidi: I have learned that having the right attitude to work means being hardworking, responsible, and willing to help.
Narrator: The classroom became neat, and everyone was happy because they worked together.
Moral Lesson: Always have the right attitude to work by being hardworking, responsible, cooperative, and punctual.
IMPORTANCE OF CREATING PLAYS WITH GOOD THEMES
Creating plays about honesty, integrity, and the right attitude to work helps pupils to:
1. Learn good moral values.
2. Develop confidence in speaking.
3. Improve communication skills.
4. Encourage teamwork.
5. Promote honesty and responsible behaviour.
6. Build self-discipline.
7. Become responsible members of society.
LESSON 3 - WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT

SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that a play is a story written to be acted before an audience. They also learned that plays can be used to teach important moral values.
Pupils explained the meanings of honesty, integrity, and right attitude to work. They learned that honesty means telling the truth, integrity means doing the right thing even when no one is watching, and right attitude to work means being hardworking, responsible, punctual, and willing to do one’s duties well.
Furthermore, pupils learned the steps involved in creating a simple play, including choosing a theme, selecting characters, writing a simple script, rehearsing, and performing before an audience.
Finally, pupils created and acted simple plays based on the themes of honesty, integrity, and right attitude to work, and understood that these values help us become responsible, trustworthy, and useful members of society.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction - The teacher asks pupils to mention good behaviours they practise at home and in school, such as telling the truth, working hard, and obeying rules. The teacher explains that these behaviours can be taught through drama and plays.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention good behaviours and discuss why they are important.
Step 2: Meaning of a Play and the Themes - The teacher explains the meaning of a play and discusses the themes of honesty, integrity, and right attitude to work with simple examples.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of a play and describe the three themes in their own words.
Step 3: Steps in Creating a Play - The teacher explains the steps involved in creating a simple play:
- Choose a theme.
- Select the characters.
- Write a simple story and dialogue.
- Rehearse the play.
- Perform it before an audience.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the steps used in creating a simple play.
Step 4: Demonstration - The teacher presents or reads a short play on honesty, integrity, or right attitude to work, showing how the characters speak and act.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen carefully, identify the characters, and state the moral lesson of the play.
Step 5: Group Activity - The teacher divides the class into four groups and assigns the following activities:
- Group 1: Create and perform a short play on honesty.
- Group 2: Create and perform a short play on integrity.
- Group 3: Create and perform a short play on right attitude to work.
- Group 4: Identify the moral lessons learned from each play and present them to the class.
Each group rehearses and performs its play before the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils work together to write, rehearse, perform, and discuss the moral lessons from their plays.
Step 6: Lesson Summary - The teacher reviews the meaning of a play, the themes of honesty, integrity, and right attitude to work, and the steps involved in creating a simple play.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the lesson.
Step 7: Evaluation - The teacher asks oral and written questions to assess pupils’ understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the evaluation questions and participate actively in the lesson.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

CULTURAL AND CREATIVE ARTS (CCA)
PRIMARY 4 - THIRD TERM - WEEK
THEME -  ARTS AND CRAFTS
PREVIOUS LESSON - Creating a Play with the Themes of Honesty, Integrity and Right Attitude to Work Primary 4 (Basic 4) Second Term Week 11 Cultural and Creative Arts
TOPIC - PRINT MATERIALS: LEAF AND THUMB PRINT
LEARNING

2. Meaning of Leaf and Thumb Print
3. Suitable Leaves for Printing
4. Materials for Leaf and Thumb Print
5. Steps in Making Leaf and Thumb Print
6. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
7. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of print making.
2. Explain the meanings of leaf print and thumb print.
3. Identify at least five suitable leaves for printing.
4. Mention the materials used for leaf and thumb printing.
5. Create simple designs using leaf print and thumb print.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about Colour in Our Environment, including the types, sources, and uses of colours, the colour wheel, and painting. They have also used colours to create simple artworks.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing pupils to print making, specifically leaf printing and thumb printing, as simple techniques for creating artistic designs.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Fresh leaves (mango, guava, cassava, hibiscus, etc.)
2. Poster paint or watercolour
3. Printing ink or stamp pad
4. Paintbrushes
5. White paper or cardboard
6. Palette or plate
7. Water container
8. Rag or tissue for cleaning
9. Samples or charts of leaf and thumb prints
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS

2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Have you ever noticed the beautiful patterns on the surface of a leaf or looked closely at your thumb? These natural patterns can be used to create attractive artworks without drawing them by hand. By applying paint or ink to a leaf or thumb and pressing it onto paper, we can produce beautiful prints and creative designs.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of print making, understand leaf print and thumb print, identify suitable leaves for printing, and create simple designs using these print-making techniques.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF PRINT MAKING
Print making is the process of creating pictures or designs by pressing an object covered with paint or ink onto a surface such as paper, fabric, or cardboard.
MEANING OF LEAF PRINT
A leaf print is a design made by applying paint or ink to a leaf and pressing it onto paper or another surface to produce the shape and pattern of the leaf.
MEANING OF THUMB PRINT
A thumb print is a design made by dipping the thumb into paint or ink and pressing it onto paper to create different shapes and artistic designs.
SUITABLE LEAVES FOR PRINTING
The following leaves are suitable for leaf printing because they have clear veins and firm surfaces:
1. Mango leaf
2. Guava leaf
3. Pawpaw leaf
4. Cassava leaf
5. Orange leaf
6. Hibiscus leaf
7. Cocoyam leaf
8. Neem leaf
9. Banana leaf (small pieces)
10. Pumpkin leaf (fresh and firm)
LESSON 2 - MATERIALS FOR LEAF AND THUMB PRINTING
1. Leaves
2. Poster paint or watercolour
3. Ink pad or printing ink
4. Thumb or finger
5. Paintbrush
6. White paper or cardboard
7. Palette or plate
8. Water
9. Rag or tissue for cleaning
STEPS IN MAKING A LEAF PRINT
1. Choose a fresh leaf with visible veins.
2. Apply paint evenly to one side of the leaf.
3. Place the painted side on paper.
4. Press the leaf gently with your hand.
5. Carefully remove the leaf to reveal the print.
6. Allow the print to dry.
STEPS IN MAKING A THUMB PRINT
1. Dip your thumb lightly into paint or ink.
2. Press your thumb gently onto paper.
3. Lift your thumb carefully.
4. Repeat to create patterns or designs.
5. Use a pencil or marker to add details if desired.
6. Allow the artwork to dry.
LESSON 3 - CREATING DESIGNS WITH LEAF AND THUMB PRINT
Pupils can create beautiful designs such as:
1. Flowers
2. Butterflies
3. Trees
4. Birds
5. Fish
6. Fruits
7. Greeting cards
8. Decorative borders
9. Nature scenes
10. Simple patterns
IMPORTANCE OF LEAF AND THUMB PRINTING
Leaf and thumb printing help pupils to:
1. Develop creativity and imagination.
2. Improve fine motor skills.
3. Appreciate nature.
4. Learn simple print-making techniques.
5. Produce attractive artworks.
6. Build confidence in art activities.
7. Make learning enjoyable.

SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that print making is the process of creating pictures or designs by transferring paint or ink from an object onto a surface such as paper or cardboard.
Pupils also learned that a leaf print is made by applying paint to a leaf and pressing it onto paper, while a thumb print is created by pressing a painted thumb onto paper to form different artistic designs.
Furthermore, pupils identified suitable leaves for printing, such as mango, guava, cassava, hibiscus, pawpaw, and orange leaves, and learned the materials needed for leaf and thumb printing.
Finally, pupils practised creating simple designs using leaf prints and thumb prints and understood that print making helps to develop creativity, improve artistic skills, and produce beautiful artworks.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction - The teacher displays different fresh leaves and samples of leaf and thumb prints. The teacher asks pupils if they have ever used leaves or their thumbs to create pictures.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the materials, share their experiences, and identify some of the leaves.
Step 2: Meaning of Print Making - The teacher explains that print making is the process of creating pictures or designs by transferring paint or ink from an object onto a surface. The teacher also explains the meanings of leaf print and thumb print.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meanings of print making, leaf print, and thumb print in their own words.
Step 3: Suitable Leaves and Materials for Printing - The teacher displays suitable leaves such as mango, guava, cassava, hibiscus, pawpaw, and orange leaves. The teacher also introduces the materials used for leaf and thumb printing.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the suitable leaves and the materials needed for print making.
Step 4: Demonstration - The teacher demonstrates how to create a leaf print and a thumb print by applying paint to a leaf or thumb and pressing it gently onto paper.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the demonstration and ask questions where necessary.
Step 5: Practical Activity - The teacher guides pupils to create simple designs such as flowers, butterflies, birds, trees, or patterns using leaf and thumb prints.
